texts.orig: This paper introduces the Human-AI Governance (HAIG) framework, contributing to the AI Governance (AIG) field by foregrounding the relational dynamics between human and AI actors rather than treating AI systems as objects of governance alone. Current categorical frameworks (e.g., 'human-in-the-loop' models) inadequately capture how AI systems evolve from 'tools' to 'partners', particularly as foundation models demonstrate emergent capabilities and multi-agent systems exhibit autonomous goal-setting behaviours. As systems are deployed across contexts, agency redistributes in complex patterns that are better represented as positions along continua rather than discrete categories. The HAIG framework operates across three levels: dimensions (Decision Authority, Process Autonomy, and Accountability Configuration), continua (continuous positional spectra along each dimension), and thresholds (critical points along the continua where governance requirements shift qualitatively). The framework's dimensional architecture is levelagnostic, applicable from individual deployment decisions and organisational governance through to sectorial comparison and national/international regulatory design. Unlike risk-based or principlebased approaches that treat governance primarily as a constraint on AI deployment, HAIG adopts a trust-utility orientation - reframing governance as the condition under which human-AI collaboration can realise its potential, calibrating oversight to specific relational contexts rather than predetermined categories. The analysis reveals how technical advances in self-supervision, reasoning authority, and distributed decision-making drive context-dependent and non-uniform evolution in trustworthiness conditions - with consequences for the trust attitudes of relevant stakeholders that existing categorical frameworks are ill-equipped to track. Case studies in healthcare and European regulation demonstrate how HAIG complements existing frameworks while offering a foundation for adaptive regulatory design that anticipates governance challenges before they emerge.

texts.text: 1. Introduction: Rethinking Human-AI Relationships

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The governance of AI systems increasingly demands frameworks capable of accounting for dynamic, non-uniform shifts in how authority, autonomy, and accountability are distributed between human and AI actors. As algorithmic systems take on greater roles in shaping decisions, allocating resources, and influencing public life, the question is not merely whether we trust them, but whether they are designed and maintained to warrant that trust. What is required is neither blind faith in machines nor paralysing scepticism, but a governance model that can continually calibrate how much trust is appropriate, and in which contexts.

texts.orig: Artificial intelligence is fundamentally reshaping the landscape of organisational decision-making, public service delivery, and institutional governance (Engin et al., 2025; Rudko et al., 2024; Shrestha et al., 2019). Across sectors, it is rapidly evolving from basic automation to increasingly sophisticated forms of governance partnership (Rahwan et al., 2019; Pedreschi et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025), aiming for human-AI complementarity where collaboration produces greater value than either alone (Stephany & Teutloff, 2024; Akata et al., 2020; Donahue et al., 2022; van Breda & Barry, 2020). This evolution is particularly evident in technical advances such as foundation models with emergent capabilities, self-supervised learning systems that critique their own outputs, and multi-agent architectures that exhibit collective behaviours beyond their individual components. These technical developments fundamentally challenge traditional governance frameworks by introducing dynamic capability boundaries and distributed agency patterns that resist static categorisation. However, our conceptual frameworks have not kept pace with this evolution (Goos & Savona, 2024).

texts.orig: This limitation becomes particularly evident as AI systems increasingly permeate domains traditionally dominated by human judgment. In healthcare, diagnostic AI systems gradually shift from flagging anomalies to making preliminary diagnoses (Yelne et al., 2023; Qiu et al., 2024); in financial services, credit algorithms evolve from augmenting human judgment to making autonomous decisions for standard applications (Gsenger & Strle, 2021); in transportation, selfdriving systems dynamically redistribute authority between human and machine based on environmental conditions (Ansari et al., 2022). Even in knowledge work requiring complex reasoning-legal practice, academic research, strategic decision-making, and creative productionAI systems now operate as collaborative partners rather than mere tools (Sowa & Przegalinska, 2025; Koehler & Sauermann, 2024), progressively assuming greater agency. Multi-agent systems embedded in infrastructure further demonstrate this evolution, with interconnected algorithms collectively reshaping environments through distributed decision-making (Cugurullo & Xu, 2025; Luusua et al., 2023; Engin et al., 2020). Perhaps most consequentially, AI is increasingly embedded in processes central to democratic governance -from content moderation that shapes public discourse, to algorithmic allocation of public resources, to automated enforcement of regulations, to decision support systems that inform policy development (Engin & Treleaven, 2019; Dunleavy & Margetts, 2023). AI systems in these contexts fundamentally challenge traditional frameworks for understanding accountability, oversight, and democratic control (Coglianese & Lehr, 2017; Gritsenko & Wood, 2020; Stokel, 2025) as they incrementally assume greater decision-making authority without corresponding evolutions in oversight frameworks.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This paper introduces the Human-AI Governance (HAIG) framework for analysing trust dynamics across evolving human-AI relationships. Situated within but extending the emerging field of AI governance (AIG), which Birkstedt et al. (2023) characterise as spanning ethical, regulatory, organisational, and technical domains, HAIG foregrounds the relational dimension: how decision authority, process autonomy, and accountability configuration are dynamically distributed between human and AI actors across evolving deployment contexts. Where existing AIG frameworks are predominantly harm-preventive - designed to identify risks, assign categories, and impose constraints on AI deployment (Kaminski, 2023; Ebers, 2024) - HAIG's trust-utility orientation reframes this: governance is not only a constraint on AI capability but a condition for realising its potential. Utility here encompasses not only technical effectiveness but democratic legitimacy and public confidence; performance gains achieved at the cost of accountability diffusion do not satisfy the trust-utility criterion. By calibrating oversight to the trust requirements of specific human-AI relationships rather than to predetermined risk categories, HAIG makes proactive governance tractable - anticipating where existing mechanisms will become insufficient before capabilities advance past them, rather than responding reactively once governance gaps have become acute. HAIG operates across three complementary levels: dimensions, continua, and thresholds, providing both theoretical comprehensiveness and practical flexibility by acknowledging continuous agency redistribution while identifying meaningful transition points requiring governance adaptation. Throughout, human-AI relationship refers to the governance relationship between human and AI actors - how authority, autonomy, and accountability are distributed across a given deployment context - rather than to the interactional or psychological dimensions of human-AI engagement.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The HAIG framework is a conceptual contribution in the tradition of integrative theory development (Jaakkola, 2020): it synthesises existing bodies of knowledge into a new analytical architecture rather than generating new empirical data. The governance gap it addresses - a structural mismatch between the continuous, multi-dimensional nature of human-AI relationships and the static categorical frameworks developed to govern them - motivates a dimensional approach in which governance relationships are represented as positions along continuous axes rather than as members of discrete categories. That gap has two structural foundations that any adequate response must address (Narayanan and Kapoor, 2024). First, risk and governance requirements are not properties of AI models but emerge from deployment context: the same system may present negligible governance concerns in one application and require stringent oversight in another. Second, unlike traditional regulatory objects such as pharmaceuticals or aircraft, AI systems are not static artefacts - they are continuously updated, fine-tuned, and version-dependent, such that a system approved or categorised under one configuration may behave substantially differently after subsequent modification. Static categorical frameworks, by design, cannot track either form of variation systematically. Dimensional positioning can.

texts.orig: Framework development proceeded through structured synthesis of three bodies of scholarship. Human-automation interaction theory (Parasuraman et al., 2000; Vagia et al., 2016; Methnani et al., 2021) provides the theoretical vocabulary for continuous representation of authority and autonomy. AI governance and regulatory scholarship (Mäntymäki et al., 2022; Birkstedt et al., 2023; Kaminski, 2023; Smuha, 2021) establishes the governance gap the framework addresses and situates HAIG primarily within the organisational and regulatory levels of AIG analysis. Trust theory as applied to automated systems (Lee & See, 2004; Toreini et al., 2020; Ferrario et al. 2024; Laux et al., 2024) grounds the trust-utility orientation and the threshold architecture. These three clusters have largely developed in parallel; their integration is itself a substantive contribution. The dimensional approach it produces is not novel in principle - Wilson et al. (2025) demonstrate its analytical value within clinical decision support - but HAIG applies it at a different level of abstraction: a cross-sector governance architecture built on three theoretically orthogonal axes of Authority, Autonomy, and Accountability (Engin & Hand, 2025).

The organisational and institutional level (Mäntymäki et al., 2022) is the primary locus of directly actionable outputs in this paper - reflected in the framework's deployment guidance (Section 4.4) and the healthcare case study (Section 5.1) - while the sectorial and national regulatory levels are addressed through Figure 2 and the EU AI Act analysis (Sections 5.2-5.3). texts.orig: HAIG's most significant limitation is the absence of longitudinal empirical validation tracking how governance frameworks evolve alongside AI capabilities across real deployments - the primary future research direction identified in Section 6. A related limitation concerns operationalisation: authority, autonomy, and accountability do not correspond to simple physical measurements, and developing robust validated measures for them is identified as important future work. The trust thresholds in Section 4.3 are designed to generate testable propositions toward this end, making specific predictions about where governance frameworks will encounter difficulty that can be evaluated against empirical evidence as it accumulates.

The recurring patterns this practice surfaces - static categorical frameworks that break down at boundaries, trust mechanisms that fail to scale, accountability structures that cannot accommodate distributed agency - are not theoretical constructs but observed governance failures that motivate the framework's design, consistent with design science approaches to framework development (Hevner et al., 2004).

texts.orig: AI integration across public and commercial domains demands new approaches to human-AI relationships (Lai et al., 2023; Rahwan, 2018; Wilson et al., 2025). This section maps the landscape of existing approaches across four strands that collectively motivate the HAIG framework - not arbitrarily, but because their limitations, taken together, define the governance gap it addresses. Governance philosophy scholarship (Section 3.1) establishes what existing regulatory approaches can and cannot do. Trust and accountability studies (Section 3.2) reveal how confidence in algorithmic systems is built and eroded over time. Agentic AI scholarship (Section 3.3) documents the technical developments outpacing those frameworks. Section 3.4 then synthesises these limitations.

texts.text: 3.1. Governance Philosophies

texts.label: text
texts.orig: As AI systems increasingly permeate decision-making contexts, several distinct governance approaches have emerged to address the challenges of human-AI relationships. These approaches reflect different priorities, disciplinary perspectives, and governance philosophies that shape how we conceptualise, implement, and regulate AI systems across society.
texts.text: As AI systems increasingly permeate decision-making contexts, several distinct governance approaches have emerged to address the challenges of human-AI relationships. These approaches reflect different priorities, disciplinary perspectives, and governance philosophies that shape how we conceptualise, implement, and regulate AI systems across society.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Risk-based approaches exemplify the tension between clarity and adaptability. The EU's AI Act categorises systems by potential harm (unacceptable to minimal risk), yet struggles with evolving systems and contextual variation (Kaminski, 2023; Laux et al., 2024). Foundation models particularly challenge this approach with their 'multifunctionality' across deployment contexts (Coglianese & Crum, 2025). Rights-based frameworks centre on protecting fundamental human rights in AI deployment (Smuha, 2021; UN Human Rights Council, 2024; Toronto Declaration, 2018). While establishing essential normative foundations, they often lack specific implementation guidance for complex socio-technical systems. Principle-based governance, advanced by organisations like the OECD and IEEE, establishes broad normative guidelines focusing on values like fairness, transparency, and accountability. While creating useful ethical frameworks, these approaches often struggle with operationalisation and enforcement in complex technical contexts (Mittelstadt, 2019). Trust-centred approaches position trust dynamics as fundamental to effective human-AI relationships. These frameworks, including work by Winfield and Jirotka (2018) and Toreini et al. (2020), address the social and psychological dimensions of how humans develop appropriate confidence in AI systems, though they sometimes lack the regulatory specificity of riskbased approaches.

texts.orig: "Levels of Automation/Autonomy" (LOA) frameworks span a spectrum from manual to autonomous operation, with automation frameworks focusing on task allocation (Parasuraman et al., 2000) whilst autonomy frameworks emphasise independent decision-making (Vagia et al., 2016). Both struggle with contextual variation, positioning systems in static categories rather than recognising their dynamic nature. Alkhatib and Bernstein's (2019) research demonstrated that real implementations manifest as a dynamic spectrum of agency. Foundation models further challenge these taxonomies-even when humans retain decision authority, they often rely on insights from opaque processes, creating information asymmetries where machines exert cognitive influence beyond what task-focused frameworks capture. These limitations suggest the need for approaches that consider not just task distribution, but the quality of agency and epistemic relationships within human-algorithm governance systems.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This section explores how trust dynamics specifically manifest in accountability frameworks and how they evolve alongside AI capabilities. Before mapping these dynamics, a conceptual distinction requires precise statement that will be held constant throughout the remainder of the paper. Trust and trustworthiness are frequently used interchangeably in the literature, but the distinction matters analytically. Trust denotes a relational attitude held by a human actor - individual, institutional, or public - characterised by willingness to rely on an AI system's outputs within a defined context (Lee & See, 2004); trustworthiness denotes a property of the system, reflecting the degree to which its technical characteristics warrant that reliance (Toreini et al., 2020; Winfield & Jirotka, 2018). The two are related but not equivalent: a technically trustworthy system may fail to achieve warranted trust if appropriate governance structures are absent, and trust may be extended to systems that do not warrant it. Accountability mechanisms, as this section explores, mediate between the two.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The concept of machine agency has evolved significantly over time, from early discussions of automation levels to today's more sophisticated understanding of fluid authority distribution. While early frameworks like Parasuraman et al.'s (2000) taxonomies introduced degrees of automation, they relied on discrete classifications that positioned systems in static categories. Bradshaw et al. (2013) advanced the field by conceptualising autonomous capabilities along continuous dimensions of 'self-directedness' and 'self-sufficiency' that adapt dynamically to changing contexts, laying groundwork for more fluid conceptions of AI agency. Wei et al. (2022) identify 'emergent abilities' in foundation models that appear non-linearly as systems scale, creating discontinuous jumps in capability requiring more nuanced governance approaches. Liu (2021) demonstrates that subtle variations in "agency locus" -whether an AI follows human-made or machine-learned rulessignificantly affect user trust and perceived uncertainty, suggesting agency exists on a spectrum rather than in discrete states.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Addressing these gaps requires disaggregating agency into its governance-relevant components rather than treating it as a unified construct. Authority concerns the legitimate entitlement to act or decide; Autonomy captures the degree to which action is self-directed rather than delegated or constrained; and Accountability addresses the attribution of responsibility for outcomes independently of both. These are analytically separable, and their separation matters: it is precisely the misalignment between them - authority without accountability, autonomy without legitimate authority - that constitutes the central governance challenge of agentic AI. Few existing frameworks address how these relationships evolve over time, connect governance requirements to specific technological capabilities, or account for the institutional dimensions that shape how authority and accountability are distributed across human-AI partnerships. The HAIG framework introduced in Section 4. addresses these gaps directly, reconceptualising governance along continuous dimensions that can capture the variable and dynamic nature of agency distribution in advanced AI systems - not by replacing the concept of agency, but by making its governancerelevant components tractable.

texts.orig: 4.1. The Three Governance Dimensions: Authority, Autonomy, and Accountability
texts.text: 4.1. The Three Governance Dimensions: Authority, Autonomy, and Accountability

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The HAIG framework operates across three governance dimensions - Decision Authority Distribution, Process Autonomy, and Accountability Configuration - each representing a continuum along which human-AI relationships transition. The selection of these three dimensions reflects two complementary considerations. First, they are theoretically orthogonal (Engin & Hand, 2025): each captures a distinct and non-reducible aspect of the governance relationship, such that a system can occupy very different positions on each axis independently (a point Figure 2 illustrates across sectors). In practice, correlations between dimensions are commonly observed, and high comovement across all three is itself a governance signal worth tracking: when authority, autonomy, and accountability migrate together without independent oversight of each, the asymmetries that HAIG is designed to detect risk going unnoticed. Second, and more fundamentally, the three dimensions correspond to the foundational questions any governance arrangement must answer: who decides (Decision Authority), how much human involvement is required in execution (Process Autonomy), and who is answerable for outcomes (Accountability Configuration). Other governancerelevant properties - transparency, explainability, contestability, fairness - are treated within HAIG as conditions that bear on how these dimensions should be configured, rather than as independent dimensions in the same sense. This framing accommodates them without inflating the framework's dimensional architecture beyond what the governance relationship itself requires.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Decision Authority Distribution: This dimension captures how decision-making authority is allocated between human and AI actors, with corresponding implications for how trust must be established and maintained. Along this continuum, authority shifts incrementally from humans to AI systems-as exemplified in the progression from medical diagnosis (where humans typically retain final authority) to content curation (where authority is often shared) to automated trading (where AI may exercise near-complete decision authority). This is distinct from epistemic authority - the capacity to generate credible knowledge claims (Ferrario et al., 2024) - which HAIG treats as a driver of decision authority migration along the continuum rather than as a primary governance dimension in its own right. Wilson et al.'s (2025) control relations typology similarly addresses authority at the level of the individual human-machine dyad - describing where override capability sits within a specific deployment - whereas HAIG's Decision Authority dimension operates at the level of governance architecture: the conditions under which any such allocation is legitimate, auditable, and revisable across contexts.

texts.orig: 4.2. Trust Dynamics Across the HAIG Continua
texts.text: 4.2. Trust Dynamics Across the HAIG Continua

texts.label: text
texts.orig: While Section 4.1 examines the fundamental dimensions of human-AI governance relationships, this section explores how trust characteristics vary as systems are positioned along those dimensions across a human-led to AI-led governance spectrum. The HAIG continua are positional rather than temporal: they describe the current distribution of authority, autonomy, and accountability in a given deployment context, not a trajectory that systems inevitably follow. The same system may occupy different positions simultaneously across deployment contexts, and movement in either direction reflects governance choices as much as technical development. That positioning is shaped by multiple factors - technological capability, organisational choice, regulatory context, and stakeholder trust - of which technical development is the most systematically studied but not the only determinant.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Among these drivers, the AI field's explicit and sustained trajectory toward greater autonomy and agency warrants particular attention. The progressive development of self-supervised learning, emergent reasoning capabilities, and multi-agent architectures reflects a deliberate research direction aimed at reducing human intervention requirements and expanding the scope of AI decision-making. This creates persistent and directional pressure on governance arrangements: as technical capabilities expand the possible range of AI authority, organisational, regulatory, and trustbased factors determine how much of that range is actually exercised in any given deployment. HAIG is designed to track that determination - not to assume it follows technological capability automatically. Critically, it is also designed to resist importing the field's own developmental narrative into the governance framework itself. When governance frameworks adopt the progressive vocabulary of the technology sector - treating greater autonomy as a natural next stage rather than a governance choice - they risk normalising a trajectory rather than evaluating it. The capability configuration framing is a deliberate methodological response to this risk: each configuration describes a cluster of technical properties and governance arrangements that tend to co-occur, without encoding any claim that movement from one to another constitutes progress in a governance-relevant sense.

texts.label: text

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This contextual variation is driven not merely by technological capabilities but by domain-specific risk tolerances, stakeholder expectations, and regulatory requirements that shape how much agency AI can exercise in different settings. This is particularly evident with foundation models, which might simultaneously operate at different positions along the decision authority continuum based solely on deployment context-not because their capabilities differ, but because the governance thresholds at which warranted trust can be sustained vary dramatically across deployment contexts. A single large language model might exercise minimal authority when providing information for research purposes, moderate authority when generating creative content for low-stakes applications, and significant authority when deployed for automated content moderation or other consequential decision-making. Similarly, healthcare AI systems might operate with high process autonomy for wellness recommendations but maintain tight human supervision for clinical interventions.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The same functional purpose can be served by systems occupying very different positions on the HAIG continua, and each positional shift carries distinct trustworthiness conditions even when the organisational mission remains constant. Medical diagnostics illustrates this clearly. The diagnostic function has remained stable across decades, but the governance position of systems serving that function has shifted substantially as rule-based expert systems have given way to statistical ML and then to foundation model-based multimodal analysis. Each configuration introduces distinct trustworthiness conditions (see Table 1) that are not reducible to one another and cannot be addressed by governance frameworks designed for a prior configuration. The application context is constant; the governance requirements are not.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Where institutions have moved through configurations in sequence, accumulated governance experience can inform trustworthiness assessment of successor configurations - transferring not the specific mechanisms but the institutional capacity to recognise when governance frameworks are becoming misaligned with technical capabilities. This is, however, the exception rather than the rule. The more consequential and more common pattern is that institutions adopt new configurations out of sequence: skipping intermediate configurations under competitive or regulatory pressure, deploying new capabilities before governance frameworks for prior configurations are fully consolidated, or finding that deep familiarity with one configuration creates institutional resistance to recognising the governance demands of a successor. In these circumstances - which are precisely the circumstances HAIG is designed to address - accumulated sequential experience is absent, partial, or actively misleading. Positional tracking across the HAIG continua matters most where orderly progression cannot be assumed, because it provides governance orientation that experience transfer cannot supply.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Configuration adoption patterns are not only non-sequential - movement along the HAIG continua is also non-uniform in direction and rate. texts.text: Configuration adoption patterns are not only non-sequential - movement along the HAIG continua is also non-uniform in direction and rate. Organisations do not simply advance toward greater AI authority and autonomy; they frequently reverse course, and they rarely progress across all three dimensions simultaneously.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Bi-directional movement is well documented in practice. Content moderation provides a clear example - several major platforms initially progressed toward AI-dominant moderation but subsequently reintroduced stronger human oversight when stakeholder trust was damaged by false positives. This reversal was not a governance failure but a governance response: public and institutional acceptance functioned as a constraint on progression regardless of technical capability, and organisations that had advanced along the Decision Authority dimension retreated when that advancement proved unsustainable. The direction of movement is therefore not simply a function of what a system can do, but of whether stakeholders will sustain the trust that expanded AI authority requires.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: While movement along the HAIG continua is continuous and bi-directional, it is not uniformly smooth. Within and between capability configurations, AI systems reach critical points where existing governance mechanisms become insufficient and qualitatively different approaches are required. These points are termed trust thresholds rather than trustworthiness thresholds because they are irreducibly relational: they mark points where shifts in system-level trustworthiness conditions interact with the trust attitudes of relevant stakeholders - institutional, professional, or public - to produce a qualitative discontinuity in governance requirements that neither dimension alone determines. Trust thresholds therefore represent not merely quantitative increases in capability or agency but qualitative shifts in the conditions under which warranted trust can be sustained, and consequently in the governance arrangements needed to maintain it. Four primary thresholds are identified, representing fundamental transitions in human-AI governance relationships, supported by several secondary thresholds that further delineate the governance landscape (Figure 3).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Healthcare AI has progressed through distinctive phases across various medical domains, with radiology serving as a particularly illustrative example. The evolution spans from rule-based clinical decision support systems with minimal decision authority (Papadopoulos et al., 2022), to advanced ML systems with greater process autonomy (Wang & Summers, 2012), to foundation model-based diagnostic partners (Qiu et al., 2024), and emerging multi-agent care coordination systems (Moritz et al., 2025). In radiology specifically, early computer-aided detection systems utilised rule-based pattern matching (Giger et al., 2008), then evolved toward convolutional neural networks requiring statistical validation (Chartrand et al., 2017), and most recently to foundation model-based diagnostic systems introducing challenges around emergent capabilities (Thieme et al., 2023)-all while serving the same fundamental diagnostic purpose. This technological evolution within a stable application context (Steiner et al., 2021) demonstrates why dimensional governance approaches provide more precise calibration than categorical frameworks.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The Decision Authority continuum in healthcare spans from purely informational systems to those with significant diagnostic authority. Examples range from basic reference tools like drug interaction databases (Knox et al., 2024), to early warning systems generating alerts (Henry et al., 2015), to diagnostic systems for standardised image interpretation with significant classification authority (McKinney et al., 2020). Stroke diagnosis AI systems exemplify this evolution, progressing from simple support tools to systems with differentiated authority based on case complexity (American Heart Organisation, 2024). Importantly, this movement is bi-directional in healthcare settings. Some systems initially progressed toward greater AI decision authority in medication management but subsequently reintroduced stronger human oversight after encountering unexpected edge cases (Lyell & Coiera, 2017), while automated sepsis alert systems were often scaled back after experiencing alert fatigue (Ginestra et al., 2019), demonstrating how organisations calibrate authority distribution through experimentation and learning.

texts.orig: 5.2. The HAIG Framework and the EU AI Act: Complementary Governance Paradigms
texts.text: 5.2. The HAIG Framework and the EU AI Act: Complementary Governance Paradigms

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The EU AI Act's risk-based categorisation (2024) and the HAIG framework's dimensional approach represent different but potentially complementary governance paradigms. Table 2 maps these two approaches across six governance elements, illustrating where they diverge and where they are most productively combined. The most fundamental difference lies in their organising logic: where the EU AI Act assigns systems to fixed risk categories with standardised requirements, HAIG tracks positional movement along continuous dimensions and calibrates governance responses accordingly. This yields contrasting approaches to adaptation and context-sensitivity - the Act reassigns systems between categories when their risk profile changes, while HAIG accommodates incremental movement and contextual variation without requiring reclassification. Crucially, these differences do not make the frameworks incompatible; rather, the EU AI Act's categorical structure provides regulatory clarity and baseline requirements, while HAIG's dimensional approach offers the finer-grained calibration that static categories cannot supply within themselves.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The HAIG framework addresses a governance deficit that the existing AI governance literature has identified but not resolved. Birkstedt et al. (2023) document persistent knowledge gaps around how governance frameworks evolve alongside AI capabilities; Laux et al. (2024) show that the EU AI Act conflates trustworthiness with acceptable risk, losing the relational dimension of trust; Coglianese and Lehr (2017) diagnose the core accountability challenge of algorithmic governance as incremental authority migration that escapes categorical notice. HAIG responds to all three. By representing governance relationships as positions along three continuous dimensions rather than as members of discrete categories, the continuum architecture tracks how authority, autonomy, and accountability are actually distributed and how that distribution evolves. Its trust-utility orientation restores the relational logic that risk-based approaches suppress. And its threshold system provides structured early warning precisely where categorical frameworks go blind: at the points where quantitative shifts in any dimension produce qualitative discontinuities in governance requirements.

texts.orig: The framework's three analytical contributions are distinct. The first is the governance asymmetry diagnostic: tracking the three dimensions simultaneously makes visible the misalignments - rapid Process Autonomy advancement against constrained Decision Authority; accountability frameworks lagging both - that single-axis approaches systematically miss. The second is the non-sequential configuration insight: institutions that adopt new AI configurations out of sequence cannot rely on accumulated governance experience to orient them, and positional tracking provides the orientation that experience transfer cannot. The third is the threshold architecture as a research programme: rather than producing principles to be endorsed or categories to be assigned, HAIG generates specific, empirically evaluable propositions about where governance mechanisms will encounter difficulty - the response to Mittelstadt's (2019) observation that principles alone cannot guarantee ethical AI.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The framework's implications differ by audience. For regulators, the EU AI Act analysis demonstrates that dimensional calibration and categorical compliance are complementary, not competing: categorical frameworks establish baseline requirements; HAIG provides the finergrained calibration within categories that static tiers structurally cannot. For deploying organisations, the key practical contribution is the diagnostic function - governance choices about how much of the authority space technical capabilities open up to actually exercise should be made deliberately, with attention to positioning across all three dimensions simultaneously. For oversight bodies, the threshold architecture offers what Coglianese and Lehr's diagnosis demands: a mechanism for anticipating authority migration rather than responding to it after the fact.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The framework's primary limitation is the absence of longitudinal empirical validation. This is also its most significant research direction: whether the trust thresholds predict governance failure points in practice, whether asymmetry patterns recur characteristically across sectors, and how institutional governance readiness mediates configuration transitions are all open empirical questions. The threshold architecture is designed to generate testable propositions toward this end. Secondary directions include operationalising dimensional measurement, extending the framework to the individual and international levels, and developing governance theory for the multi-agent frontier that the Individual to Collective AI threshold marks.

HAIG is designed to make that alignment trackable.

● Process transparency: Systems can be explicitly inspected and their logic verified ● Direct verification: Outputs can be comprehensively checked against expected results ● Clear boundaries: System limitations and constraints are well-defined and understood ● Stable behaviour: System performance remains consistent and predictable over time

● Statistical reliability: Consistent performance across varied scenarios ● Pattern recognition validity: Accurate identification of relevant patterns in data ● Appropriate confidence levels: Well-calibrated certainty in system outputs ● Effective exception handling: Reliable identification of cases requiring human attention

● Capability boundary understanding: Clarity about system capabilities and limitations ● Alignment verification: Demonstration of consistent value alignment ● Adaptation governance: Controlled and monitored system learning ● Supply chain integrity: Trustworthiness of model sources and training processes

● Emergent behaviour governance: Management of collective system behaviours ● Bounded autonomy: Appropriate constraints on autonomous operations ● Systemic resilience: Reliable operation under unexpected conditions ● Value alignment: Consistent adherence to societal values across operations
